I've saved the answers to `/work/answer.json`. I checked the order count and found no 'paid' orders without line items, so the per-order average (g) has no denominator problem.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| a. Segment with the highest Q3 net sales | `enterprise`, 311,006,588원 |
| b. Customers with a paid order in Q3 | 247 |
| c. Category with the highest Q3 net sales | `svc`, 342,643,721원 |
| d. Month with the highest net sales, all periods | 2025-07 |
| e. Customer with the largest Q3 refund total | u42@ex.com (2,803,550원) |
| f. Customers with 2 or more paid orders in Q3 | 232 |
| g. Average net sales per paid Q3 order | 699,410원 (869,367,528원 ÷ 1,243 orders) |
| h. Net sales growth, August to September | 2.6% (280,191,709원 → 287,379,540원) |

Two points could change the answers:
- **Segment for a:** 50 accounts share an email with another account, and some of those groups have different segments (for example, u101@ex.com has accounts in both smb and enterprise). For a, I used the segment of the account that placed each order. Merging accounts by email only applies to the customer counts (b, f) and to grouping refunds by email (e). If you want one segment per person, you'd need a rule for which one to pick, and the a total could change.
- **Refunds:** I subtracted refunds from the order's own sales (the order-date month), not from the month the refund happened. The refunds table has no refund date, so the refund-month approach wasn't possible.

The data is otherwise clean: every refund matches an order line and no refund is larger than its line quantity. I converted dates to KST by adding 9 hours.
